In this profile it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the other items, whereas the other maladaptive strategies center on vigilance, escape, and social evaluation.

vignette: Kamal had always taken pride in his independence and self-reliance. As an auditor, he was meticulous and detail-oriented, able to navigate complex financial records with ease. But all of that changed on a night out with friends at a local club. It started like any other night - laughter, music, and dancing - but ended in a bathroom stall, where Kamal was brutally raped by a stranger. The smell of cheap cologne still made his stomach turn, transporting him back to that moment of utter helplessness. He would catch whiffs of it on the street, in elevators, or at parties, and suddenly he'd be frozen in time, reliving the terror. People misbehaving - whether it was someone cutting in line or honking aggressively in traffic - also triggered a visceral response in Kamal. He saw the world as a chaotic, unpredictable place where anyone could become a predator. Kamal's relationships suffered as well. When people made casual references to his ex, he felt like he'd been punched in the gut. It was as if they were taunting him, reminding him of his own vulnerability. His friends and family noticed the change in him - the constant looking over his shoulder, the quick exits from social gatherings - but Kamal couldn't explain it to them. In an effort to regain some sense of control, Kamal started taking certain precautions. He always made sure to stay close to an exit, whether he was at a restaurant or a friend's house. This way, he could make a swift escape if needed. Situations where others evaluated him - his appearance, his performance, his worth - became unbearable. Job reviews with his boss left him sweaty and anxious; even compliments from strangers made him cringe. Kamal started wearing loose-fitting clothes to avoid drawing attention to himself. Baggy shirts and jeans became his armor, protecting him from the prying eyes of others. He felt like a ghost hovering on the periphery of social interactions, invisible but constantly vigilant. The world had become a minefield for Kamal, full of potential threats waiting to be triggered. Unfamiliar places made him anxious - how could he assess the danger if he didn't know the layout? Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard; a friend's playful tap on the shoulder would send his heart racing. Kamal felt like his body was constantly on high alert, tense and ready to react to any perceived threat. His muscles ached from being coiled for so long, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Self-doubt crept in, too. Kamal couldn't shake the feeling that someone else - anyone else - would have avoided getting into this situation. He replayed the night of the assault over and over in his head, wondering what he could've done differently. He used to be a happy person, full of laughter and optimism, but now misery clung to him like a shroud. The sense of humiliation lingered, a festering wound that refused to heal. Kamal felt permanently tainted by the experience, as if he'd been branded with an invisible scar. His eyes would well up with tears when no one was looking, overwhelmed by the weight of his own shame. It took months for Kamal's loved ones to notice the toll this had taken on him. They staged an intervention, urging him to seek help before it was too late. What finally brought Kamal to therapy was a panic attack at work - he'd been reviewing financial records when a coworker approached him with a question, and suddenly he was back in that bathroom stall, fighting for air. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kamal knew what he wanted: to find a way out of this darkness, to rediscover the carefree person he once was. What he feared most was losing himself completely, becoming forever trapped in this prison of his own making.
